raw_response:
I farm only 5.5 mu, so I cannot take big risks. I still do the usual wheat-maize rotation. That is the safest for our family here in Quzhou. I have middle school education, so I do listen to what the extension people say, but in the end I still go by what I saw on my own land. In these years, if wheat gets enough base fertilizer and one good topdressing, the stand is steadier. Maize also cannot be delayed after wheat harvest, or yield drops fast. Some people in my family work off-farm, so labor is tight at busy times. Because of that, I keep the plan simple, use improved seed, split fertilizer into the key times, and irrigate when it really matters. We have well water, but pumping costs money, so I will not water too many times unless the season turns dry.

For wheat, I will sow in early October, about the usual time in the village. I will use a common improved wheat seed from the local dealer, not the most expensive one. Before sowing, I will put most of the phosphorus and part of the nitrogen down as base fertilizer, because if I skip that, wheat starts weak and tillers poorly. Then at jointing I will topdress again if the wheat color is not deep enough. I plan about three irrigations if the weather is normal: one after sowing if soil moisture is short, one around jointing, and one around grain filling. For maize, I will plant right after wheat harvest in mid-June, with almost no delay. That turnaround is always tight, so I will keep tillage light and hire machine work if needed. I will use hybrid maize seed because local seed is not worth saving for maize. I will put fertilizer once at planting and once around the big flare stage, and usually irrigate once if rain is not enough. I would rather spend a bit on fertilizer than let the crop turn yellow and lose yield, but I still have to watch cash because the farm is small.
